oxigeno.name: 🫁 Oxygen cartridge
oxigeno.desc: +20 oxygen; helps when levels are low.

1.title: Aurora of Luna-7
1.description: The crew ends safe and with important science results.

2.title: Star garden
2.description: The greenhouse and supplies are ready for the next crew.

3.title: Knowledge for Earth
3.description: The mission brings valuable research despite the difficulties.

4.title: The bridge restored
4.description: Communication lets the team plan the next phase of the mission.

5.title: A united crew
5.description: Teamwork and care for each other held the base together.

6.title: Imperfect rescue
6.description: The mission ends with difficulties and a support plan.

7.title: Controlled silence
7.description: The team stays safe, but the link with Earth is still at risk.

8.title: Emergency retreat
8.description: The crew stops the science mission and starts emergency procedures.

9.title: Silence in the habitat
9.description: A serious life-support crisis ends with the loss of an astronaut and the end of the mission.

10.title: The last walk
10.description: A spacewalk with a compromised suit ends with the loss of an astronaut.

donki.answer: DONKI keeps records and analysis of solar events, such as solar energetic particles (SEP) and coronal mass ejections (CME). An alert is a reason to check the shelter plan and outdoor tasks. The exact Moon risk needs more calculations.

oxygen.answer: Life support does more than add oxygen. It also controls the air and helps remove carbon dioxide. If there is a leak, adding oxygen does not replace fixing the source of the loss.
oxygen.source: NASA Open Science / educational material for the task

plant.answer: A crop needs water, light, nutrients and a controlled environment. Using more water does not guarantee better growth. Base food includes reserves, because a newly planted seed is not harvested right away.

comms.answer: A radio message takes a little over one second to travel between Earth and the Moon: 1.35 s on November 14, 2026, with the Moon at 405,616 km (NASA/JPL Horizons). Between November and December 2026 it goes from 1.19 to 1.36 s. So if contact is lost for minutes or hours, the cause is something else: antennas, pointing, power or procedures. In the game, turn delays are a simplification.
comms.source: NASA/JPL Horizons · Earth–Moon distance and light time

power.answer: A battery stores energy; it does not make it. If several systems use power at the same time, you must decide which load comes first. To protect the crew, life-support functions usually come first.
power.source: NASA · power challenges of a Moon base

radiation.answer: The CRaTER instrument, on board the LRO orbiter that circles the Moon, measures radiation. On a normal day (January 2020) it read 13.22 microgray per hour. During the solar storm of September 11, 2017 it reached 19,481.6 microgray per hour: about 1,732 times normal, because the Moon has no atmosphere and no global magnetic field to protect it. These are measurements in lunar orbit, not inside a habitat; that is why a base needs a shelter.
radiation.source: NASA OSDR RadLab · LRO CRaTER (lunar orbit)

sources.answer: In Vita Lunae, we tell apart NASA historical records, science explanations and numbers made up for the game. A DONKI solar event is not a dose measured directly inside a lunar habitat.

1.name: Air check
1.intro: The ventilation system shows an odd reading. Should you check before going outside to explore?
1.cause: Start of the mission: first check of the habitat.
1.science: Air quality depends on several systems. One reading is not enough to find the cause.

choices.label: Calibrate sensors and filters
choices.consequence: Air becomes stable, but maintenance uses energy.

choices.label: Trust the indicator
choices.consequence: You save energy today, but CO₂ can build up tomorrow and cause headaches.

2.name: A dosimeter blinks
2.intro: One astronaut's meter shows an odd reading before a spacewalk.
2.cause: As she gets close to the suit area.
2.science: Dosimeters record exposure. An odd value must be checked against context and the instrument.

choices.label: Check the instrument
choices.consequence: The spacewalk is delayed, and the team learns how to check a measurement.

choices.label: Go out without checking
choices.consequence: The mission saves time, but uncertainty about exposure grows.

3.name: Dust on the panels
3.intro: Some solar panels give less energy than expected.
3.science: Light, angle and wear all affect solar power. Dust is a maintenance problem.

choices.label: Clean with the robot
choices.consequence: Production recovers, at the cost of a small battery reserve.

choices.label: Overload the system
choices.consequence: Energy rises for a moment, but one piece of equipment is strained.

4.name: First seeds
4.intro: The greenhouse has limited water and trays ready for a first experiment.
4.cause: On your first visit to the greenhouse.
4.science: Real food production takes time: the 'food' meter includes reserves and production capacity.

choices.label: Plant with controlled watering
choices.consequence: The farming experiment moves ahead, but the water goes down.

choices.label: Save all the water
choices.consequence: Reserves are kept, but crop research is delayed.

5.name: First message from Earth
5.intro: The crew receives instructions and photos; the antenna battery is needed for other things too.
5.science: The normal Earth–Moon signal delay is about 1.3 seconds one way. Longer interruptions need another cause.

choices.label: Send a short transmission
choices.consequence: Earth learns the base status, at a cost in energy.

choices.label: Postpone the transmission
choices.consequence: Power is saved, but pending reports pile up.

6.name: Clogged filter
6.intro: The life-support module warns that the filter needs attention.
6.science: Ventilation and CO₂ removal are part of life support, not just the oxygen supply.

choices.label: Replace the cartridge
choices.consequence: The air improves and the risk of symptoms drops.

choices.label: Reduce ventilation
choices.consequence: Energy is saved, but breathing discomfort can appear.

7.name: Outing under watch
7.intro: Researchers report more solar activity. A trip outside is about to start.
7.cause: As she gets ready to leave the habitat.
7.science: The risk depends on the solar event, the location and the shielding. The game simplifies these variables.

choices.label: Reschedule the trip
choices.consequence: The crew stays protected, but a work window is lost.

choices.label: Make the trip short
choices.consequence: A sample is collected, but exposure risks go up.

8.name: Backup battery
8.intro: A freshly checked battery can power the water recycler or the lab.
8.cause: When the first electrical reserve is assigned.
8.science: A battery stores energy; it does not create it.

choices.label: Prioritize the recycler
choices.consequence: Water is recovered; research is delayed.

choices.label: Turn on the lab
choices.consequence: Science data is gathered, but there is less electrical margin.

9.name: Uneven sprouts
9.intro: Some seedlings grow worse than others in the greenhouse.
9.science: Plant growth depends together on light, water, nutrients and the environment.

choices.label: Check light and nutrients
choices.consequence: The setup is fixed, though it takes time and energy.

choices.label: Increase watering without measuring
choices.consequence: Some plants improve, but water is wasted and contamination may appear.

10.name: The reply is late
10.intro: Earth's confirmation has not arrived. Is it normal delay or a link failure?
10.science: A delay of about 1.3 s each way does not explain a loss of communication lasting minutes or hours.

choices.label: Check the signal log
choices.consequence: An antenna needs adjusting, and rushed decisions are avoided.

choices.label: Repeat messages nonstop
choices.consequence: Congestion grows and energy is used up without fixing the fault.

11.name: Headache
11.intro: An astronaut has a headache and tiredness. The crew suspects an air or rest problem.
11.cause: If air quality or workload is ignored.
11.science: Symptoms are not specific. In the game, the team looks for the cause instead of making a diagnosis.

choices.label: Check the air and rest
choices.consequence: Well-being improves, at a cost in energy and time.

choices.label: Ask her to keep going
choices.consequence: Productivity holds for now, but a crisis may appear.

12.name: Suit with damaged protection
12.intro: A warning says the exploration suit's protection may be compromised.
12.science: A spacesuit protects against several dangers; radiation is only one of them.

choices.label: Inspect and replace parts
choices.consequence: Safety improves, using materials and energy.

choices.label: Use it for one last mission
choices.consequence: A sample is collected, but the risk to the person going out rises.

13.name: Power spike
13.intro: The recycler, greenhouse and fans all need electricity at the same time.
13.cause: When three systems run at once.
13.science: A microgrid design must balance generation, storage and demand.

choices.label: Schedule use in turns
choices.consequence: Total load drops and energy is saved, though research moves more slowly.

choices.label: Keep everything on
choices.consequence: Production continues, but the electrical margin gets worse.

14.name: Water for whom?
14.intro: The lab asks for watering water while life support needs reserves to run.
14.cause: When the stored water is shared out.
14.science: On a lunar base, water must be counted for drinking, hygiene, recycling and technical processes.

choices.label: Assign measured watering
choices.consequence: The crop is protected, with a moderate drop in water.

choices.label: Save water for the crew
choices.consequence: The immediate risk drops, but the crop is at risk.

15.name: Misaligned antenna
15.intro: Module movement or a pointing fault reduces link quality.
15.science: Link geometry and pointing affect communications. Not every delay is normal latency.

choices.label: Recalibrate from inside
choices.consequence: Communication returns and the fault is recorded.

choices.label: Wait for another window
choices.consequence: Electricity is saved, but a critical order may arrive late.

16.name: Pressure microleak
16.intro: A sensor detects a slow loss in one compartment of the habitat.
16.science: In a pressurized habitat, a leak must be found: making more oxygen does not fix the cause.

choices.label: Isolate and repair the section
choices.consequence: The air is kept; the team gives up energy and time.

choices.label: Make up the loss with more supply
choices.consequence: The problem stays open and uses up reserves every shift.

17.name: Historic solar alert
17.intro: The observatory reports a solar event recorded by NASA DONKI as a training scenario.
17.science: DONKI reports historic solar events. It does not turn an event into an exact dose on the Moon by itself.

choices.label: Activate shelter protocol
choices.consequence: Risk drops, and the protection system uses energy.

choices.label: Continue outdoor tasks
choices.consequence: Field science is gained, but a higher simulated exposure is accepted.

18.name: The crater's shadow
18.intro: The Sun's position leaves a set of panels in shadow during a work window.
18.cause: As the base nears a poorly lit area.
18.science: On the Moon, shadows and light cycles directly affect solar power.

choices.label: Move robots and share out the load
choices.consequence: Power is rebalanced, though oxygen and electricity are used in operations.

choices.label: Keep every load on
choices.consequence: The battery runs down faster and the blackout risk rises.

19.name: Crop contamination
19.intro: Signs that may mean contamination are seen in a hydroponic tray.
19.cause: If sanitary control is not enough.
19.science: Food hygiene and monitoring of closed systems are crucial in space environments.

choices.label: Isolate the suspect trays
choices.consequence: Part of the crop is lost, but the rest and health are protected.

choices.label: Mix the whole harvest
choices.consequence: The immediate loss is avoided, but the stored food could be at risk.

20.name: Contradictory orders
20.intro: Two messages arrive out of order and suggest different priorities.
20.science: Space communication needs checkable messages and autonomous procedures for failures.

choices.label: Check the time stamps
choices.consequence: The crew clears up the order of events and coordinates better.

choices.label: Run the newest message on screen
choices.consequence: Delay is avoided, but a team may shut down a needed system.

21.name: Water recycler
21.intro: The system recovers less water than planned and the tanks are going down.
21.cause: When the water reserve falls or a fault appears.
21.science: Recycling saves resources, but it needs maintenance and energy.

choices.label: Change the recovery circuit
choices.consequence: Water is recovered and safety improves, using electricity.

choices.label: Ration without repairing
choices.consequence: Energy is saved, but fatigue rises and output falls.

22.name: Design a shelter
22.intro: The base must choose which compartment to use as a shelter during a solar event.
22.science: How much shielding material there is, and where it sits, affects protection. The simulator uses an abstract scale.

choices.label: Protect a small space
choices.consequence: Crew protection improves, but activities are limited.

choices.label: Spread materials across the whole base
choices.consequence: Mobility is kept, but effective protection is not enough.

23.name: Partial blackout
23.intro: One circuit shuts off, leaving part of the greenhouse and one fan without power.
23.cause: After an overload or low battery levels.
23.science: Restoring in stages helps keep critical loads under control.

choices.label: Restart by sectors
choices.consequence: Life support is stabilized, at a cost in food and productivity.

choices.label: Force a full restart
choices.consequence: It is faster, but the fault can spread to other systems.

24.name: Wilting plants
24.intro: Water, light or temperature in the greenhouse are not well balanced.
24.science: Visible plant symptoms have many causes: observing before acting avoids waste.

choices.label: Diagnose the cause
choices.consequence: Conditions are fixed before using more resources.

choices.label: Increase all supplies
choices.consequence: The crop improves in the short term, but reserves run out faster.

25.name: Unstable link
25.intro: The base loses contact at times, and an outdoor activity depends on an order.
25.cause: When the link with Earth fails on and off.
25.science: Operational independence matters because immediate control from Earth is not always possible.

choices.label: Activate autonomous protocol
choices.consequence: The crew can keep going with safety rules and send fewer messages.

choices.label: Wait with no backup plan
choices.consequence: The team loses time, stress rises and a repair is delayed.

26.name: Hard breathing
26.intro: Two crew members feel dizzy and have breathing discomfort during a task.
26.cause: If air quality gets worse or symptoms are not treated.
26.science: Signs of discomfort call for checking life support and safety, not an automatic diagnosis of a specific illness.

choices.label: Stop work and check the air
choices.consequence: An air problem is found and safety is restored.

choices.label: Keep going until done
choices.consequence: Time is saved, but the team's physical state gets worse.

27.name: Built-up exposure
27.intro: A dosimeter summary shows that spacewalk planning must be reviewed.
27.cause: After several spacewalks or a solar event.
27.science: Accumulated exposure must be compared with limits and conditions. The game does not calculate clinical doses.

choices.label: Cut spacewalks and check protection
choices.consequence: The team protects its health, though a science mission is lost.

choices.label: Prioritize the findings
choices.consequence: More data is collected, at a cost to safety.

28.name: Power sharing
28.intro: Scientists want to turn on a new instrument just as the batteries are running low.
28.cause: When several tasks compete for the same supply.
28.science: Energy management is an optimization problem with limits and goals that pull in different directions.

choices.label: Assign quotas per system
choices.consequence: Water and air get priority without fully canceling the science.

choices.label: Give the instrument full priority
choices.consequence: Research moves ahead, but electrical reserves are stretched thin.

29.name: Biofilm in the pipes
29.intro: A biofilm may be in part of the watering line, and the food system must be protected.
29.cause: If there are hygiene or watering failures.
29.science: Water and food systems in closed environments need microbiological monitoring.

choices.label: Isolate and disinfect the circuit
choices.consequence: Production is lost, but health is protected and the team learns from the incident.

choices.label: Use the circuit to the end
choices.consequence: Temporary production is kept, but the health risk goes up.

30.name: Critical transmission
30.intro: Earth asks for a report to plan possible help. The link needs power priority.
30.cause: When an emergency balance must be sent.
30.science: Sending reliable information matters as much as sending it fast.

choices.label: Send a compressed report
choices.consequence: The base's situation becomes clear and coordination becomes more likely.

choices.label: Save battery for life support
choices.consequence: Air is protected, but Earth gets incomplete information.

31.name: Crew fatigue
31.intro: One astronaut is exhausted and makes procedure mistakes.
31.cause: After several days of too many tasks.
31.science: Rest, teamwork and behavioral health are part of space planning.

choices.label: Cut shifts and look after the team
choices.consequence: Health improves and mistakes become less likely, but output is delayed.

choices.label: Extend the shifts
choices.consequence: Short-term productivity rises, but fatigue grows and morale drops.

32.name: Spacewalk during alert
32.intro: A team is outside when a warning arrives that needs a coordinated response.
32.cause: During outdoor trips with higher risk.
32.science: During a space weather alert, protection and the return procedure are key.

choices.label: Return now and shelter
choices.consequence: The task is left unfinished, but safety improves.

choices.label: Finish the task first
choices.consequence: Information is gathered, but the crew faces a bigger danger.

33.name: Central grid failure
33.intro: A distribution fault threatens to cut off water, communications and ventilation.
33.cause: If an overload is not fixed in time.
33.science: Redundancy stops a single failure from halting the whole mission.

choices.label: Build an emergency microgrid
choices.consequence: Critical systems stay on, though research is paused.

choices.label: Keep running on a single circuit
choices.consequence: The restart seems fast, but if it fails again, several systems are hit.

34.name: The last harvest
34.intro: Trays grown before the mission began can add food, but they must be inspected.
34.cause: When reserves run out and some crops are already ripe.
34.science: A harvest in seven days is only plausible for plants that were already growing; a crop started on day 1 does not ripen all at once.

choices.label: Harvest only what is safe
choices.consequence: A modest reserve is gained and health is protected.

choices.label: Harvest everything without inspection
choices.consequence: The reserve grows, but there is a risk of stomach upset from compromised food.

35.name: Ask for evacuation?
35.intro: The team must decide whether to ask for an early return or keep waiting for supplies.
35.cause: Under uncertainty about reserves and the connection.
35.science: The decision to end a mission must consider safety, logistics and checkable communications.

choices.label: Ask for help with full data
choices.consequence: Earth can plan a response; the communications reserve is used up.

choices.label: Keep the mission without reporting
choices.consequence: Energy and autonomy are kept, but possible help is delayed.

36.name: Life-support crisis
36.intro: Two essential systems fail at the same time and the operating margin is minimal.
36.cause: If air and water problems pile up.
36.science: In emergency operations, the priority is keeping critical systems running, not maximizing research.

choices.label: Apply the emergency protocol
choices.consequence: Air and water come first, at the cost of energy and experiments.

choices.label: Improvise to save the experiments
choices.consequence: Scientific data is kept, but the base's safety is compromised.

37.name: Severe solar event
37.intro: The team faces an extreme scenario based on space weather science records.
37.cause: During a serious alert in an advanced stage.
37.science: Radiation scenarios are educational: they do not replace specific lunar dose calculations.

choices.label: Stay in the protected shelter
choices.consequence: The crew lowers the risk, though power output drops and activities are lost.

choices.label: Go out and repair right now
choices.consequence: Part of the energy is recovered, at the cost of greater simulated exposure.

38.name: Extreme rationing
38.intro: Few electrical reserves are left and three important systems need power.
38.cause: When solar output no longer covers demand.
38.science: With limited resources, you must decide which loads are critical and which can wait.

choices.label: Keep air and water first
choices.consequence: Life support is saved and secondary tasks are suspended.

choices.label: Feed all tasks equally
choices.consequence: No system gets enough and the risk of total blackout rises.

39.name: Seeds or food
39.intro: Reserves are limited: the crew must decide what to keep for the base's future.
39.cause: When you must choose between short and long term.
39.science: Food security combines immediate availability and the resilience of the production system.

choices.label: Save seeds and ration
choices.consequence: Long-term sustainability is protected, but immediate food drops.

choices.label: Eat all available reserves
choices.consequence: Immediate food improves, but the ability to keep growing is sacrificed.

40.name: The last contact window
40.intro: At the end of the mission, Earth needs a final report to plan the next step.
40.cause: As the campaign nears its end.
40.science: The quality of a mission also depends on recording and communicating what was learned.

choices.label: Send telemetry and decisions
choices.consequence: Learning is documented and coordination improves, at a cost in electricity.

choices.label: Save the remaining energy
choices.consequence: The last energy reserve is protected, but Earth gets less information.

41.name: Water to make oxygen
41.intro: The electrolysis oxygen generator needs water while the consumption tanks go down.
41.cause: The oxygen tank enters high-demand mode.
41.science: Electrolysis needs water and electricity. The simulation simplifies the real flows.

choices.label: Adjust output and recover water
choices.consequence: The system keeps the air with controlled use of the tanks.

choices.label: Demand maximum output
choices.consequence: Oxygen rises, but water reserves run out and a crisis begins.

42.name: Lost dosimeter report
42.intro: A scientist lost the dose history before planning a new trip outside.
42.cause: A radiation alert coincides with spacewalk planning.
42.science: Dose readings let teams make informed decisions; by themselves they do not predict an outcome.

choices.label: Rebuild the readings and stop the spacewalk
choices.consequence: The team is protected and the report is documented.

choices.label: Approve it without history
choices.consequence: The expedition moves up, but the unassessed risk remains.

43.name: The module dilemma
43.intro: Only enough power is left to keep two of three modules on: recycler, crop and antenna.
43.cause: Demand is higher than the power available.
43.science: Electrical management must put critical loads first, not just comfort.

choices.label: Prioritize recycler and antenna
choices.consequence: The crew keeps water and contact; the crops are delayed.

choices.label: Prioritize crop and lab
choices.consequence: Science moves ahead and food reserves grow, but distribution fails.

44.name: Missing nutrients
44.intro: The plants are alive, but the hydroponic system has the wrong nutrient mix.
44.science: Hydroponics depends on water, nutrients and microbial control.

choices.label: Analyze the solution and correct the doses
choices.consequence: The crop is stabilized, using energy and materials.

choices.label: Use an unchecked mix
choices.consequence: It seems to save time, but it puts the trays at risk and adds uncertainty.

45.name: Duplicate message: a real order?
45.intro: A repeated instruction arrives and the team does not know if it fits the current situation.
45.cause: Two communication packets seem to contradict each other.
45.science: The physical Earth–Moon delay is not the same as a fault or a duplicate message.

choices.label: Check the time stamp and version
choices.consequence: They avoid running an order twice and keep a backup.

choices.label: Run it without checking
choices.consequence: Priorities get mixed up and the network gets even more congested.

46.name: Medical module decompression
46.intro: A seal fails. The pressure drops and an astronaut needs immediate help.
46.cause: After a leak is ignored or a compromised seal is detected.
46.science: Depressurization can quickly harm life support; its numbers are simplified.

choices.label: Seal, isolate and assist
choices.consequence: The losses are contained; health needs watching.

choices.label: Delay the isolation
choices.consequence: The leak gets worse, confusion appears and the crew is at risk.

47.name: Return from the crater
47.intro: An astronaut is far from the base when a danger warning arrives and a seal problem is found in her suit.
47.cause: Radiation warnings and suit faults pile up.
47.science: A badly sealed suit brings immediate risks of pressure and oxygen loss. The solar event gives context to the decision, but no lethal dose is inferred.

choices.label: Return with rover help
choices.consequence: The astronaut gets back to a safe area; the expedition is cut short.

choices.label: Finish collecting
choices.consequence: The spacewalk drags on with a compromised suit and the risk becomes extreme.

48.name: Cascading blackout
48.intro: The grid is overloaded. The fan, recycler and communications are about to stop.
48.cause: Poor load balance and earlier faults combine.
48.science: Without stable power distribution, life-support equipment can be affected.

choices.label: Isolate circuits and restart
choices.consequence: Basic functions come back, and research is limited.

choices.label: Restart everything at once
choices.consequence: The overload hits three systems and the effects on the crew speed up.

49.name: Suspicious ration
49.intro: Two crew members have stomach upset after sharing food that may be contaminated.
49.cause: The greenhouse had cleaning and storage problems.
49.science: When food contamination is suspected, the product is identified and isolated; you do not diagnose from symptoms alone.

choices.label: Isolate the food and give help
choices.consequence: More exposure is avoided, though some food is lost.

choices.label: Keep handing out rations
choices.consequence: More symptoms appear and work capacity drops.

50.name: The last order with no reply
50.intro: The base must coordinate an evacuation; the link is intermittent and a new instruction may not arrive in time.
50.cause: The team built up delays or electrical and antenna problems.
50.science: Crew independence is essential because communication can be lost.

choices.label: Apply the local plan and send a signal
choices.consequence: Operational independence is kept and the best available report is sent.

choices.label: Wait without acting
choices.consequence: Critical reserves run out and rescue is delayed.
